title: Super Ugly Number
statement:
Call a positive integer *super ugly* when every prime dividing it is one of the values in `primes`. The number `1` has no prime divisors at all, so it always qualifies. Write all super ugly numbers in increasing order and return the `n`-th one, counting from 1.

`primes` lists distinct primes in ascending order, and the inputs guarantee that the answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer.
constraints: Every primes[i] is a prime number
primes is strictly increasing (its values are unique and sorted)
The n-th super ugly number is at most 2^31 - 1
notes:
## Intuition

Every super ugly number other than `1` is a smaller super ugly number multiplied by one of the primes. So for each prime `p`, the values `ugly[0]·p, ugly[1]·p, ugly[2]·p, ...` form an increasing stream, and the whole sequence is the merge of these streams. Testing integers one by one is hopeless (the answer can be near 2^31); building the sequence in order costs only O(n·k).

## Approach

1. Create `ugly` with `ugly[0] = 1`. For each prime `j`, `index[j]` points at the number it will multiply next and `candidate[j] = ugly[index[j]] * primes[j]` is the head of its stream (initially the prime itself).
2. For each position `i` from 1 to `n - 1`, the smallest candidate is the next super ugly number; store it in `ugly[i]`.
3. Advance **every** prime whose candidate equals that value: bump `index[j]` and recompute `candidate[j]`. Advancing all ties keeps duplicates out.
4. Return `ugly[n - 1]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`primes = [2, 7, 13, 19]`, candidates start at `[2, 7, 13, 19]`. The minimum `2` becomes `ugly[1]` and the 2-stream moves to `2·2 = 4`. Then `4` (2-stream moves to `8`), `7` (7-stream to `14`), `8`, `13`, `14`, `16`, `19`, `26`, `28`, `32`. The list is now `[1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 13, 14, 16, 19, 26, 28, 32]`, and the 12th value is `32`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n·k) for `k = primes.length`: each of the `n` steps scans all candidates twice.
- Space: O(n + k) for `ugly`, `index` and `candidate`.

## Pitfalls

- When two primes produce the same value (`2·7` and `7·2`), advance both, or `14` appears twice.
- Candidates can exceed 2^31 even though the answer does not; in Java or C, store them in a 64-bit type.
- `1` is the first super ugly number, so `n = 1` returns `1` without any work.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ugly` | the super ugly numbers found so far, in increasing order |
| `index[j]` | position in `ugly` that prime `j` multiplies next |
| `candidate[j]` | `ugly[index[j]] * primes[j]`, the next value prime `j` offers |
| `next` | the smallest candidate, the next super ugly number |
| `i`, `j` | the position being filled and the prime being examined |

narration.2: Allocate room for the first n super ugly numbers.
narration.4: Every prime starts by multiplying ugly[0].
narration.5: Each prime's first offer is the prime itself, 1 times p.
narration.7: Fill positions 1 through n - 1 in increasing order.
narration.8: Look for the smallest offer among all primes.
narration.10: Keep the minimum candidate seen so far.
narration.12: The smallest offer is the next super ugly number.
narration.14: Every prime that offered this value must move on, so duplicates never appear.
narration.15: Point this prime at the next number in the list.
narration.16: Its new offer is that number times the prime.
narration.20: The last value filled is the n-th super ugly number.
